title: Zoho's Sridhar Vembu Warns AI Is Choking IT Job Creation for India's Youth
excerpt: The Zoho founder says companies are diverting hiring budgets to AI infrastructure, urging students to think twice before taking on massive education loans in a shrinking job market.
body:
• Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI is fundamentally reshaping India's IT workforce, with companies cutting new hiring to fund AI infrastructure.
  • Entry-level tech hiring at the 15 largest firms fell 25% between 2023 and 2024, and the trend has accelerated through 2026.
  • TCS has cut 12,000 jobs while Microsoft laid off 15,000 employees even as it poured $80 billion into AI — a pattern Vembu calls a direct budget trade-off.
  • Vembu urged companies to fund training programs and accept alternative credentials rather than trapping young Indians in crippling education debt.

Sridhar Vembu, the founder and chief scientist of Zoho Corporation, has issued one of his most pointed warnings yet about the impact of artificial intelligence on India's technology workforce, calling the slowdown in IT job creation "the real issue facing our nation."

In a series of posts on X and remarks at industry events, Vembu argued that the AI boom is not merely automating tasks — it is fundamentally redirecting corporate budgets away from hiring and toward expensive infrastructure, leaving millions of young Indians staring at a job market that no longer needs them in the numbers it once did.

The Budget Trade-Off

Vembu's core argument challenges the popular narrative that AI is simply replacing workers with smarter software. The reality, he contends, is more structural: companies are slashing headcount to pay for the servers, GPUs, and data centres required to run AI systems.

"Companies are blaming job losses on AI, which is both convenient, and as an added bonus, makes a company look visionary."

— Sridhar Vembu, Founder and Chief Scientist, Zoho Corporation

The numbers support his case. TCS announced layoffs of roughly 12,000 employees — about 2% of its global workforce — in mid-2026. Microsoft cut 15,000 jobs in 2025 while simultaneously committing $80 billion to AI development. Entry-level hiring across the 15 largest technology companies dropped 25% between 2023 and 2024, according to industry data, and the decline has only steepened.

A Harvard study tracking 62 million workers found that when companies adopt generative AI, junior developer employment drops by 9–10% within six quarters, while senior employment remains essentially flat. Companies are not firing juniors so much as choosing never to hire them.

The Productivity Paradox

Vembu has spoken from experience at his own company. He described a senior engineer in Zoho's R&D division who independently built an advanced assembly and machine-code security tool in a single month — work that would traditionally have required a team of three to four engineers over a year. That represents a roughly 12-fold productivity gain from one experienced engineer armed with AI tools.

But the gains come with a catch. Effective use of AI requires deep domain knowledge and years of hands-on experience — precisely the kind of expertise that junior engineers once acquired through the routine work AI now handles. The entry ramp into the profession is disappearing even as the profession itself grows more productive.

Vembu compared the moment to Indian IT's "textile industry moment," drawing a parallel to the era when large-scale manual weaving gave way to mechanised production, displacing millions before new forms of work eventually emerged.

A Warning on Education Debt

The Zoho founder has been particularly blunt about the financial risks facing students. Citing the case of a student who took on ₹70 lakh ($80,000) in debt at 12% interest to pursue a master's degree at a small American college, Vembu said Zoho itself could not offer relief because the company has pulled back on hiring as it transforms for the AI era.

"I urge students and parents to be cautious in borrowing heavily to pursue degrees abroad and in India. We should not trap young people in debt in the name of education."

— Sridhar Vembu, on X

His proposed alternative: employers should fund training programs directly, and the broader industry should accept alternative credentials rather than demanding formal degrees that saddle graduates with debt they may never repay in a tightened market.

A Global Pattern Hits Home

The trends Vembu describes are not confined to India. California, Oregon, and Washington — the heartland of the American tech industry — tied for the second-highest unemployment rate in the United States in June at 5.2%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists attribute the spike directly to AI-driven hiring slowdowns in software development, data analysis, and IT support, according to CNN.

For India, the stakes are amplified by scale. The country produces over 1.5 million engineering graduates annually, and the IT services sector has long served as the primary employment engine for this cohort. If that engine stalls, the ripple effects extend well beyond technology into education, real estate, and consumer spending in cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune.

What Comes Next

Vembu has stopped short of predicting catastrophe. He has noted that history shows large-scale technological shifts "create more jobs than they destroy" and has urged software engineers to develop stronger customer relationships rather than relying solely on coding skills. At a recent AI Summit, he told The Hindu BusinessLine that AI models from companies like Anthropic have accelerated prototyping dramatically, compressing months of work into days.

But his broader message is cautionary. He has questioned the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending spree, aligning with IBM CEO Arvind Krishna's warning that the multi-trillion-dollar data centre build-out may be a bubble. Zoho, he said, will invest in capabilities like data curation and reinforcement learning but "will not chase the investment bubble."

For the millions of young Indians planning careers in technology, the message is sobering: the industry that lifted a generation into the middle class is undergoing its most profound structural shift in decades, and the old playbook — degree, campus placement, steady IT job — may no longer apply.
